prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

All my life I was face to face with her, at meal-times, by the fire, even in the ultimate intimacies of the bed. You could have asked, then, for information about her? There was a room apart she kept herself in, teasing me by leading me to its glass door, only to confront me with my reflection. I learned from her even so. Walking her shore I found things cast up from her depths that spoke to me of another order, worshipper as I was of untamed nature. She fetched her treasures from art’s storehouse: pieces of old lace, delicate as frost; china from a forgotten period; a purse more valuable than anything it could contain. Coming in from the fields with my offering of flowers I found her garden had forestalled me in providing civilities for my desk. ‘Tell me about life,’ I would say, ‘you who were its messenger in the delivery of our child.’ Her eyes had a fine shame, remembering her privacy being invaded from further off than she expected. ‘Do you think death is the end?’ frivolously I would ask her. I recall now the swiftness of its arrival wrenching her lip down, and how the upper remained firm, reticent as the bud that is the precursor of the flower.

Keywords: All, You, There

outputs.L2: Throughout my entire existence, she stood before me—during our meals, beside the hearth, and even in the deepest closeness of our shared bed. Surely, you'd think, I could tell you everything about her? Yet she kept a private chamber all to herself, taunting me by drawing me toward its glass door, where all I could see staring back was my own image. Still, she taught me things. As I wandered along her coastline, I discovered objects washed up from her hidden depths, and these hinted at some different realm—I who so devoted myself to wild, untamed nature. Her prizes came from the vaults of art: fragments of aged lace, fragile as morning frost; porcelain from some bygone age; a handbag worth more than whatever might be tucked inside it. When I returned from the meadows bearing flowers as my gift, I discovered that her own garden had already beaten me to it, having furnished my desk with its graceful gestures. "Speak to me of life," I would ask her, "you who announced its coming when you brought our child into being." A delicate embarrassment would fill her gaze, as she recalled how her solitude had been breached from a greater distance than she had anticipated. "Is death truly the finish of it all?" I would tease. Even now I remember how quickly the answer came, pulling her lower lip downward, while her upper lip stayed steady and reserved, silent as the bud that comes before the bloom.
outputs.L3:
Throughout the entirety of my life, I existed in constant physical closeness to a certain woman. We shared the same spaces, breathed the same air, and moved through the days in near-perpetual proximity to one another. And yet, for all that nearness, I never truly knew her. Her inner world remained a mystery to me, sealed and impenetrable, no matter how many years we spent side by side.

She was, by nature, a secretive presence. It often seemed as though, whenever I sought to look deeper into who she was, she would lead me only back to my own reflection—showing me myself rather than herself. But even in that guardedness, she was not without her gifts. From her, however indirectly, I learned a great deal. She taught me not through open confession, but through the quiet example of how she lived and what she valued.

For she possessed a refined and cultivated appreciation for art and beauty. She surrounded herself with treasures and shared them freely: delicate old lace, antique china of exquisite craftsmanship, and the flowers she coaxed from her garden with patient devotion. In these small, cultivated pleasures, she revealed a sensibility that spoke of an inner richness I could sense but never fully grasp.

Again and again, I came to her with my questions. I asked her about the great mysteries—about the meaning of life, about the nature of death, about all the things that lay beyond my understanding. In my mind, she was a kind of messenger, someone who stood closer to those deeper truths than I did, someone who might, if only she chose to, unveil the answers I so desperately sought.

But her death, when it came, arrived without warning. It was sudden, abrupt, final. And in that final moment, her expression froze upon her face in a way I have never forgotten—an expression that seemed to hold within it two things at once: the certainty of an ending, and the ache of a promise left unfulfilled. Whatever secrets she had carried, whatever answers she might one day have given me, she took with her into silence.
outputs.L4:
# The Unknowable

I knew her all my life, and yet I never knew her at all. This is the paradox I have carried like a stone in my chest—that a person could stand so close to me, breath against breath, and still remain a country I was never permitted to enter.

There were rooms inside her I sensed but never saw. I imagined them sometimes: chambers behind chambers, doors that opened only onto other doors, each one locked with a key she kept hidden even from herself. I would knock, in my quiet ways—a question asked at the right moment, a silence held open like a palm—hoping she might step through and show me what lay behind her eyes. But she would only smile, or turn away, or answer with a warmth that was itself a kind of wall. I learned to love the wall. What else could I do?

When I looked at her, I saw myself reflected back. Perhaps that was the trick of it—that her surface was so polished, so complete, that I mistook my own longing for her depths. I studied the reflection for years. I called it understanding. Only later did I realize I had been looking at glass the whole time, and that the woman behind it had gone about her private business, unseen, unguessed.

She gave me things. Not confessions—she was never generous with those—but tokens, offerings, small treasures that seemed to hint at the inner life she guarded. A shell she had carried from some far shore. A pressed flower brittle as a whisper. A stone, ordinary and gray, that she kept on the sill as though it held a meaning she alone could read. Paintings she loved, music she returned to, lines of poetry she recited when she thought no one was listening. I gathered these clues like a scholar, arranging them, rearranging them, certain that if I only found the pattern I would finally know her. But the pattern never came. The treasures were beautiful, and they were mute. They told me everything about what she valued and nothing about who she was.

And then she died.

There was no warning worthy of the name. One ordinary morning the world simply took her, quickly, cruelly, with the indifference of a door slammed by wind. I had always believed there would be time—time enough, at the end, for the walls to come down, for the hidden rooms to open, for her to turn to me at last and say *here, this is who I have been.* I had staked my patience on that final revelation. It never arrived. She left the way she had lived: complete unto herself, sealed, carrying her mysteries out of the world exactly as she had carried them through it.

Now I hold her treasures in my hands—the shell, the flower, the gray and silent stone—and I understand what I refused to understand while she lived. We do not know one another. Not truly. Not even those we love the most, those whose faces we could draw in the dark, whose voices we would recognize among a thousand. We spend our lives pressed against the surfaces of other souls, mistaking nearness for knowledge, and we go on believing that intimacy is the same as understanding until death corrects us.

She was the closest person to me in all the world. And she remains, even now, a stranger I loved with everything I had. Perhaps that is the truest thing I can say about any of us: that we are known only in fragments, guessed at, reflected, never wholly seen—and that this, too, is a kind of love, the only kind we are given, the love that reaches and reaches and never quite arrives.
outputs.L5:
# All You Need Is Already There

Sometimes we spend our whole lives searching for something that feels just out of reach. We look outward, believing that happiness, success, or purpose exists somewhere far away—in a different city, a better job, or a future version of ourselves. Yet the truth is often simpler than we imagine.

**All** of us carry within a quiet strength we rarely acknowledge. It shows up in the small moments: the decision to keep going after a setback, the courage to be kind when it's difficult, the patience to start again. These qualities aren't reserved for a special few. They belong to everyone, waiting to be recognized and used.

**You** are more capable than you often give yourself credit for. The doubts that whisper "not good enough" are not facts—they are simply fears wearing convincing disguises. When you choose to move forward despite them, you discover abilities you never knew you had. Growth doesn't require you to become someone else; it asks only that you become more fully yourself.

**There** is a place where all of this comes together—not a physical destination, but a state of mind. It's the moment you stop chasing and start appreciating. It's found in gratitude for what you have, in presence with the people around you, and in trust that you are exactly where you need to be right now.

So take a breath. Look around. Everything you need to begin is already here, and the person capable of using it is already you.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem addressed to a deceased wife, exploring intimacy, mystery, and the unknowability of another person, in the style of R.S. Thomas.
counterfactuals.output:
# Comes the Silence

You were always the far field I could not cross, the light that fell on the other side of the wall I built between us, thinking it a bridge.

Now you have gone into the deepest privacy of all, and I understand at last that I knew you the way a man knows the sea—the surface of you, the weather of your moods, the tides I learned to read but never the cold dark of your going down, the pressure of those depths where you kept whatever it was you kept.

We slept a lifetime back to back, two questions no answer would fit. I would wake in the night to your breathing and think: *there*, that is the whole of her, that rising and falling. As if breath were confession. As if the body did not keep its own counsel even in sleep.

What did you think, those evenings by the window, when the light went out of the garden and you did not turn to me? I asked, once. You smiled. And the smile was a door closing softly, the way you closed all doors—without violence, without a sound, leaving me on the outside of you where I had always, it seems, been standing.

God, they tell me, knows us utterly. I never learned the trick of it. Forty years and I could not have told you the colour of your own silence, whether it was grief in there, or peace, or some third thing with no name I had the wit to give it.

Now the house holds your absence the way a shell holds the sound of what has left it. I put my ear to the emptiness. I listen for you.

And still—*still*—you will not say.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a lyrical reflection in which a widower speaks about his late wife, using imagery of the sea, art, and a garden to convey how well and how little he knew her.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Tide Left

I knew the harbor of her,
the safe anchorage where I moored each evening—
the particular grey of her eyes at dusk,
how she took her tea half-cold,
the small country of her hands.

But the sea of her went out past sight.

---

She was a painting I lived inside,
so close I could not name the colors,
only the warmth of them,
the way morning through the kitchen
made her ordinary and gold.

Now I stand back, as one must
before a canvas, and I see
the brushwork I had missed—
the darker underpainting,
the places where she'd scraped a whole life down
and started it again in secret.

Who was the woman before I framed her?

---

She kept a garden I called *hers*
and thought I understood.
I knew the roses, yes—
I planted half of them.

But there were seeds she sowed
in soil I never turned,
things that bloomed
only when I was away,
or sleeping, or too sure.

I find them now, going through the beds:
some flower with no name I know,
tenacious in a corner,
that she must have loved
and never mentioned once.

---

The tide comes in. The tide goes out.

I loved the shoreline of her—
that meeting-place where she gave herself to me,
the wet sand printed with our years.

But I begin to understand
the ocean does not belong
to the man who walks its edge,
and the deepest part of anyone
is water we were never meant
to fathom,

only to stand beside,
and marvel,
and be grateful
for the wave that reached us,

and let go
the ones that didn't.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poetic meditation on marriage and mortality, where the speaker recalls asking his wife about life and death, ending with the moment of her stroke or death.
counterfactuals.output:
# What She Said

I asked her once, in the ordinary dark
before sleep took us under, *what do you think
happens after?* Her breath was even, warm
against my shoulder. *Nothing,* she said. *Or everything.
The same to us who won't be here to know.*

We had been married then for thirty years.
Long enough to speak in fragments, to leave
sentences unfinished on the table
like a shared meal, each knowing what the other meant.

I asked her if she feared it. Feeling her shrug,
that small seismograph of her whole self,
I felt her turn the question over like a stone
found on a beach, examined, then returned.
*I fear the leaving,* she said. *Not the gone.*

How casually we spend our afternoons
as if they came in some unending stock,
as if the body were a house we'd always own
and not a borrowed room, the lease unread.

This morning she was standing at the sink.
The light came ordinary through the glass.
She was saying something about the garden, how
the tomatoes had come in early this year, how—

and then the word broke off. The cup she held
did not so much fall as forget her hand.
I watched her face become a country
where the roads were being erased, one by one,
her mouth still shaping language that had left.

*I fear the leaving,* she had said. And now
I understood: she meant this. She meant me,
standing here, unable to follow where
she went so quickly, the whole of her
poured out through some invisible fracture in the light.

Nothing, she'd said. Or everything.

I hold her hand. It is still warm.
I am still asking. She has stopped
answering, or has answered, finally,
in the one language I was never taught to read.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an introspective piece in second person and first person that treats a woman as an enigma the narrator lived beside for a lifetime, blending domestic detail with metaphysical questions.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Woman in the Next Room

You were always just beyond the doorway, and I have spent a lifetime learning the geography of your absence even as you filled the house with the smell of bread, of woodsmoke, of the lavender you pressed between the pages of books you never let me read.

I know the sound of your feet on the third stair. I know you take your tea with too much sugar and pretend otherwise to the doctor. I know these things the way I know the arrangement of my own bones—without ever having seen them, without ever being sure they are truly mine.

But who were you, in the dark, when you thought I slept?

---

I would watch you at the window some mornings, holding a cup gone cold, looking at something in the garden that was not the garden. Where did you go? I built a life beside you—forty-one winters, the children we buried and the children we raised, the mortgage, the quarrels about money, the reconciliations we performed without words. And still you kept a room in yourself I was never given the key to.

You are the great unsolved thing of my existence. Not a mystery to be cracked—I gave up detective work years ago—but a mystery to be lived alongside, the way a man lives beside a mountain and calls it *home* though he has climbed no more than its lowest slope.

---

Consider the ordinary facts:

That you folded the laundry in a particular way, corners meeting corners, a small daily insistence on order in a disordered universe.

That you hummed when you were frightened.

That you touched the doorframe each time you entered a room, a superstition you inherited from a mother you claimed not to love.

I collected these like a naturalist, thinking that if I gathered enough of them I might arrive at *you*. As if a woman were the sum of her habits. As if the soul could be assembled from evidence.

---

But here is the metaphysics of it, the thing that keeps me awake now that you are gone and the house has learned a terrible silence:

**If I never knew you—not truly, not to the marrow—then what was it I loved for forty-one years?**

Was it a portrait I painted and hung where you stood? Did I marry a real woman or my long dream of her? And if the latter, were you doing the same? Were we two strangers, each in love with an invention, passing the sugar, sharing the bed, growing old across the vast diplomatic distance between one consciousness and another?

I think now that this is the condition of all love. Not failure. Just the truth of it. We are each of us sealed vessels, sending signals through the hull. That you remained unknown to me does not mean I failed to know you. It means you were *real*—too real, too infinite, to be contained in any knowing.

---

You in the kitchen. You with flour on your wrists. You singing that song whose words I never caught.

I lived beside a wonder and called it *wife*, called it *the years*, called it *ordinary*, because I did not have the courage to call it what it was: a presence I could not fathom, sleeping an arm's length away, breathing the same night air, and utterly, gorgeously, unreachably other.

---

The tea things are still where you left them.

I have not moved the cup.

And when I pass the doorway to the next room, I still feel you there—just beyond it, just out of sight, holding something I was never meant to hold, looking at a garden that was never only a garden.

I touch the doorframe now.

I have taken up your superstitions, one by one, as though by living your small rituals I might finally enter the room where you kept yourself.

But the room is empty.

And still I do not know if you have left it, or if you were never, in the way I needed, there at all.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a short elegiac prose passage about lifelong companionship, unknowability, and loss, rich with metaphors of nature versus art and imagery of buds and flowers.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Grafted Rose

We were planted in the same season, you and I, our roots drinking from one dark soil, and for sixty years I believed I knew the shape of you as I knew my own hand closing in sleep. But a person is not a garden one may walk at leisure. You were the wilder thing, the hedgerow rose that would not be trained against the trellis I so carefully built, and though I pruned and coaxed and tied you to my straight ambitions, some green and secret part of you climbed always toward a light I could not see.

How I labored to make an art of you. I wanted the cultivated bloom, the flower pressed flat and named in the book of my understanding. Yet you remained the bud that never fully opened to my looking—closed not from coldness but from that soft unknowable center every living thing folds around itself, the mystery no lover's patience may unfurl.

I thought I had all the summers. I thought the petals would keep.

Now you are gone into the earth that made us both, and I am left holding the empty trellis, the artificer whose subject has returned to nature. The frost has come early to my little plot. And I understand, too late, that I loved not the rose I imagined but the rose that was—untamed, unfinished, and forever just beyond the reach of my knowing hands.

Bloom on, wherever you have gone. I will tend the ground until I follow.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
